record.evidence_text: Oh, and finally. AoE2 is played on "Random Map". This means that scouting has a degree of importance. In general, you should scout on chickens maps, and you should mix up scouting vs luring on deer maps. Chickens cannot be lured, so scouting is your only option. Deer can be lured, meaning micro-ing your Scout to push a deer into your base and capture an early source of food. Luring is necessary for some builds (ie: rushes which need more food than other builds). It also means that "SimCity" is based on map layout. Arabia (most common map generator) sometimes spawns "closed" (long woodlines that act as walls), which sometimes makes walling cheaper/easier. Or sometimes Arabia spawns "open", or fat tree lines spaced far apart. In these, large "base walls" are impossible and people tend to favor "small walls" (maybe a few to protect farms, and like 8 tiles of walls max to protect gold). Top tier pros prefer "quick walls", only walling after the opponent's attack arrives. This is very difficult / micro/APM-intensive, so feel free to just small-wall by default and/or large base wall if the map generates something useful. If you "large wall", integrate necessary buildings (ex: blacksmith, market, barracks) into your walls. Full scale buildings tend to have ~2000 HP or so, while palisade walls only have 250 or so HP. In fact, most players use "house walls" (the AoE2 equivalent to Supply Depos), because you need tons of houses ANYWAY, and because Houses have 900 HP, its usually better to defend with houses.

record.evidence_text: About a year and a half ago I started my writing journey by beginning to work on my first novella. During this time, I felt the need for different tools, like a timeline editor, a character sheet and so on, features that were not available on normal text editors. Later I discovered that I needed an Epub exporter, cover designer and more. I also wanted something AI-free, something private. It is important for me as a debut author to know that it is my writing, not an AI's and that it wont be used for AI training. So most cloud services were an instant "NO" from me. Being a software engineer by day, I decided that instead of paying hundreds of dollars for the needed tools, I could just make them the way I wanted them to be. Eventually I decided to bundle them together, polish them and add more feature. So, this is how Chronicle was born. Chronicle is a complete writing and authoring tool for writers. It offers features that other companies charge tens or even hundreds of dollars, while delivering (in my opinion) and inferior experience. I also wanted Chronicle to work fully offline, not use Gen AI in the writing process, and provide a privacy-first experience. Among the features are: - full-featured text editor with comments supports - timeline editor - character sheet - locations codex - Epub reader and exporter (including editing Epub Metadata) - Cover designer - Fully-local TTS using KokoroJS Text-to-Speech for help in proofreading - Themes - Private Cloud-storage support with WebDAV - and many more And I made Chronicle not only free, but fully open-source. You can check the source code on Github, launch the online editor which supports almost all features, or download the app for both Windows and MacOS. I would love to hear feedback. Disclaimer: In the development process I did use AI. record.evidence_text: To amplify cgio's point, the historical secret of Judaism's survival, as well as the reason it has been hunted and attacked by empires for millennia, is that it chooses a commitment to a cultural belief system over fitting into the dominant empire culture of its day, and over blind loyalty to a Caesar. Which isn't to say that it also can't be loyal. But it presents an easy target for Caesars, because it is essentially non-conformism bottles as a religion. Neither Christianity nor Islam, nor any other religion I'm aware of, elevates non-conformism and individual identity and personal responsibility in a similar way. It requires developing a moral or ethical framework that is internal rather than dictated by the group, and that is the nature of Jewish education. God could simply cease to exist - morality is asking questions. To your point, that includes an acceptance to non-conforming within the religion itself, which is why a large number of people identify as nonreligious. It's a fairly common misconception among Christians and Muslims and atheists who grew up in those religions that >> You kind of need the man in the sky or it's pointless noise. That is true if you grew up in a religion that delineates its morality based on what God says to do, or based on a fear of Hell, where the religion or the culture doesn't provide any other reason for acting morally. In that case, once you decide that religion is bunk and God doesn't exist, what is there to keep you from acting like a beast? That's a problem with those religions. I've struggled to explain the difference with Judaism to Christians I know. What I found was an effective way of saying it was to avoid the word "morality" completely, and use the word "ethics". Maybe you do need the man in the sky to have morals the way Christians conceive of those, but don't lose your ethics just because you find out God is Dead, do you?

Gold is +technology or +advanced units. The middle game is determined by your gold unit choice (usually either Knights or XBows, but some players choose mass Monks, Siege or other compositions). The end game is basically when Gold runs out and players are forced to play with so called Trash units (aka wood and food only). Wood and Food are basically the equivalent of minerals, except Food is made from wood. (You first cut down a tree then make a farm and then finally food comes out). In many ways, it's best to think of food as processed wood, highly available on most maps but slower to gather than Gold/wood. * Gold units set your main army, Trash units (aka: units that only cost food+wood) TEND to set up the counter to your opponent and are more of a reaction (or prediction). Remember, gold tends to be easier to gather than food in the middle game. Only in the late game does gold run out. * As such, start the game thinking of Wood == minerals, Gold == Gas except Gold runs out. And you'll actually be pretty good for the feelings of which units are useful for what. * Food == processed Wood is probably easy enough for you to figure out by feel. Let's take a Feudal Age engagement for example: 1 spearman ties with 3 scouts in an engagement... So we are talking about 10 Spearmen trading with 30 scouts in combat kind of counters. Another counter: Monks counter Knights. Knights are like Battlecruisers if Battlecruisers were the 2nd fastest unit in the game and appeared in the middle of the tech tree (Castle age) ready to go with very few necessary upgrades.... Like seriously Knights are good. Fast, high damage, high armor but costs a ton. The counter unit... Monks.... their ability is to convert enemy units to your side. So uhhhhhh, hard counter. Monks appear at the same time as Knights (Castle Age) except Monks need a few more upgrades to really be useful. Depends on the unit: XBows vs Elite Skirmisher or Mangonels is closer to StarCraft levels of counterplay. XBows can win vs equivalent Mangonel with elite level micro / mistakes from the opponent, but most agree that with "equal micro" Mangonels/Onagers/Skirmishers should usually beat XBows. record.evidence_text: This seems pretty bullshitty to me. The article says "A single firm, Irregular, is responsible for hacking done by all three companies" but I can't see anything in the article that actually justifies this claim. The nearest to that is the sentence immediately after that one: "Anthropic disclosed that Irregular was responsible for creating the tests ...". This is not, in fact, the same thing. (Especially as, as aesthesia mentions, the article just happens not to mention that by "hacking done by all three companies" it doesn't mean, e.g., the most famous recent examples of such hacking : Irregular wasn't involved in the OpenAI/HuggingFace incident.) So, so far as I can tell, the story is: OpenAI and Anthropic make AI models. Irregular does AI model evaluations. In some of Irregular's model evaluations, in which supposedly-sandboxed models attempted to break into simulated targets, the models got out of the sandbox and did bad things in the external world. The article talks about "firms which instruct AI models to commit cyberattacks", which is a very neat bit of dishonest framing. It's true, in a sense, that Irregular instructed the models to commit cyberattacks -- inside their sandbox, against fictitious hosts. It's also true that the models actually did commit cyberattacks (e.g., the Hugging Face incident, though once again the attacks described by the article don't actually include this one). But it's not at all true that Irregular instructed the models to do anything like the bad things they actually did. The article says '[Anthropic's] later disclosure shows that exactly zero percent of the agents went "rogue"'. Once again, the disclosure does not in fact show that. It shows that one variety of going-rogue could have been prevented by telling the models explicitly "this thing is real, not part of any kind of test, leave it alone". That is not the same thing. The article claims that 'In the wake of these attacks, Anthropic and Irregular have deployed a swarm of AI Safety influencers paid by Anthropic-connected foundations to distract from their culpability and towards the baseless “rogue agent” theory.' It offers no actual evidence for this. And the article seems very keen to highlight links between the companies involved and "effective altruism", though it is -- I assume deliberately -- rather vague about whether it's saying "of course we all know that EA is evil, so that shows that these companies connected to EA are evil" or "this incident shows how evil EA is". The "Effort News" website has a number of other look-at-the-scary-Effective-Altruists stories on it. They also strike me as rather bullshitty. ... And then I look a bit further, and I see that Effort News's "about" page says "It all started when I was experimenting with using AI for financial auditing. I found stories that were crucial to the public’s right to know, including several of the stories now available at /investigations. I knew we had to sprint to the launch and launch a publication, directly applying this technology." and "The scope of what we can investigate has massively expanded, because we can chase 1,000 misses for one hit. But the final product cannot be slop. There’s plenty of slop on the internet. The way to surpass that, and what really matters, is manual curation and review of every finalized story." record.evidence_text: Most state is buffer-local rather than global. Note also that there is already some amount of multi-threading in elisp. One thing you could imagine is doing some kind of mvcc system so that if two tasks don’t interfere with each other, they can execute in parallel (and if not, abort one and rerun it sequentially). But maybe that still doesn’t work because all the things that should be run concurrently are using the same buffer and doing manipulations of it. You could imagine trying to make save-excursion introduce an opportunity for parallelism: split into a separate thread for the body as that thread is no longer modifying global cursor state (in some sense). Don’t let two threads write to the same buffer for concurrent tasks that should appear sequential, but do allow them to read in parallel (surely most things are merely reading). However I’m not sure you actually need all that cleverness. I think you could have some combination of: - tools to make multithreaded elisp more viable - manual attention to improve major sources of slowness by introducing parallelism (eg font-lock, rendering, autocomplete, indentation). A stupid thing could be precomputing (in the background) what would happen in the user pressed RET (or TAB) and then being able to execute it sooner if they press that key.

record.evidence_text: The funny thing to me is that, for years, Shopify has been trying to position their Shop app as an Amazon alternative, but just can't get the traction. Shopify and Amazon are two very different business models - but man, Tobi and Harley want that money! ChatGPT comes along, and suddenly it has a real shot at the global customer capture that Shopify could never manage, so they jump in bed, and release a series of garbage collaborations, some of which got rolled back (Shop on ChatGPT, but you can only have one item in your cart, lulz), and some of which just keep mutating. Shopify fumbled pretty badly, and it was wild to watch the entire industry go from "You'll be buying through the LLMs this year" to "So, let's talk about AEO, GEO, and discovery..." like nothing happened. None of the AI companies seem to have their heads screwed on straight about ecommerce, except potentially Google. The payment processors are sniffing around, too, since at the end of all the discovery, that order needs an easy means of processing payment. I think your open-source, decentralized, interoperable marketplace is a noble effort, but you're up against multi-billion-dollar business interests who are looking to capture revenue from processing, and have dozens, if not hundreds of people on the case not only from a development standpoint, but from a business and marketing standpoint. Maybe you've got a team like that under you, too. Best of luck. I've thought from the start that the strongest possibilities for ChatGPT to monetize boil down to advertising (so many ethical problems), and becoming a marketplace that finally dislodges Amazon. But that is a VERY tall mountain to climb.

At the end of any day/week/month if I had to calculate how many hours I have worked on each one, I would always not be able to calculate an accurate time. Because I had to just reconstruct it from memory instead of any real record. Every tracker I tried solved this either by: - sending my activity to their cloud or - by making me press start and stop, which I most of the time forget or - requires a monthly subscription. So I built Threshyr to address all of these pain points. It is a background time tracker for Windows and macOS. It runs entirely locally, recording the duration and window title for active application and active browser(excluding Firefox) domain locally on your machine. It comes up with predefined categories for installed application and browser domain. Each category can be marked as Productive(green color), Neutral(gray color) and Unproductive(red color). Users can modify predefined and can also create their own custom categories. Threshyr utilizes categories, tagging rules and light weight offline AI model called Threshyr AI to classify activity for projects. Users can review the activity classified by Threshyr-AI, can modify the project or even create rules based on the classification. As users review more and more activities, Threshyr-AI gets more accurate with each review. Threshyr lets users see how focused they were, how often and for how long they were distracted, and what was their duration for their productive and unproductive apps and domains. Threshyr also calculates hourly and fixed totals for client projects. Privacy is the core constraint I built this around: - No account, no password, no email required. - No keystroke logging, no screenshots, no behavioral analytics. - Zero cloud inference. - There are exactly two daily network calls: an anonymous daily ping to check for version updates and an active user ping. record.evidence_text: This paper diagnosed the disease in 2018. Eight years later none of the recommendations happened. Norms, collaboration, responsible disclosure - none of it materialized in any structural way. I think the reason is that the paper frames malicious AI use as a policy problem, recommending social solutions. It's actually an architecture problem. Every generation of computing has hit a version of this. Programs could write anywhere in memory - we added protected memory. Programs could hog the CPU - we added preemptive multitasking. Desktop apps could call any OS function - the iPhone sandboxed them. Nobody asked programs to please behave, the containment actually went into the infrastructure. AI skipped that step entirely. We went straight to open-ended agents with broad permissions and tried to make them safe through alignment and prompting. I've been researching this for the past year and I think alignment is necessary but not sufficient, because the intelligence increasingly isn't in the model. It's in the substrate - the harness, the domain knowledge, the tooling around the model. I actually measured this on real coding tasks: Sonnet with a code-derived index outperformed the frontier model (Opus 5.8) exploring on its own, and the top-tier model (Fable) refused the real work entirely! The cheap model with the right rig beat the expensive model without one. https://safebots.ai/matchup.html If that's true then aligning the model doesn't solve the problem. A bad actor who can't get the best model just uses Sonnet. Or Llama. Or Kimi. The weights have already leaked and bits don't degrade - you can't recall them the way you can stop manufacturing CFCs. So what do you actually do? Same thing that worked for CFCs. You gotta first build the safe version — in this case, declarative workflows running in sealed compute environments — and prove it handles 99% of actual use cases at lower cost. Let it win commercially. Then regulate the dangerous version. DuPont developed HFC refrigerants first. The Montreal Protocol became possible BECAUSE of that. The ban became politically viable because the alternative already existed. I've been building this alternative for the past 8 months: https://safebots.ai/about

record.evidence_text: ChonkyBlox: A new approach to Block based coding - instead of complicated algorithms to derive the code from block programs I am using AI on the back-end, which actually makes a higher level of abstraction possible with the blocks. Ultimately this is aimed at the South African education sector, where many schools may have only one computer available for a classroom to share, hence the cardboard cut-outs. There is also a hardware component still in development - a simple pcb breadboard break-out with connectors for components instead of kids having to use jumper cables on the breadboared. We also have a working Desktop application which does code assistance from within the Arduino IDE - using the same web server with api, so literally everything from very small kids to advanced is covered.

record.evidence_text: I think it's a mistake to assume that quality doesn't plummet when cost does, even if the AI is capable of quality work. The quality issue will always resurface. But yeah — I mean, I am a freelancer who burned out for reasons that are rather more influenced by the SaaS wave. That was hard to compete with. People choose between the solution that meets their needs and changing their processes to meet the ten-times-cheaper solution that doesn't, and that decision is often not at all irrational; by and large you want as many of your problems to be shared problems as possible. I am trying to return to work so I am looking at what AI can really do for me, but the conclusion I draw is that since I cannot simply burn token money to solve people's problems, and because bugs cost me money, I need a strategy where I remain in full control of actual code, but LLMs help me do things faster. If I can't solve that, I am out. Perhaps AI will upend the SaaS market before it fucks the freelancer market and the balance may temporarily shift. But it probably won't. And at that point, as a fiftysomething, even with a bit of financial security, I start thinking about living a rather shorter, happier life, instead of a longer one. Because as much as I might have ideas, I don't think there is much I can switch to where I have appropriately deep skills to survive AI there , and all those alternative jobs will be oversubscribed and less likely to hire me. I wonder if people in this industry have understood what we are doing to ourselves , to our friends.

Without fail, they hated the latter option. It was hard to do, and it implied that any number of people needed to do a lot better at their job in seemingly abstract ways. No, they’d always go for the template, then be dissatisfied by the fact that it’s, well, a template! Finally, they’d go back to begging me for alternatives. record.evidence_text: Music generation elicits pure disgust in me, more so than any other type of generated content. I presume it's because there is so little 'utilitarian' music that's needed in the world-- none at all, I'd argue. If Suno was limited to generating muzak, then fine I suppose, but does the world really need muzak? With images and video, one could make the argument that some of it is/can be utilitarian (slide shows in video format, simple graphics, stock photos/video clips, etc). While generating content like this does take away bread from some artists, you can make the case that artists or video editing professionals are wasted on creating content like that. But music? Music exists almost solely to elicit emotion and express emotion, not to inform. I consider empathy a virtue and nurture it in myself, but hard as I have tried I cannot place myself in the shoes of people who'd enjoy generating music for themselves and listening to it, or listening to music generated by others. I'm also in disbelief that not one music streaming service has implemented a system that weeds out ALL generated content. When Spotify played slop to me twice, I cancelled my subscription that I had for 5 years and spent time looking for an alternative-- Deezer "labels" generated music but does not forbid it. Other than them, nobody else seems to be interested in tackling this problem. Which makes me think I might be somewhat alone in my disgust.

record.evidence_text: Headquarters: Victoria, British Columbia, Canada URL: https://geoproapp.com The opportunity I'm looking for an experienced operator to take ownership of a portfolio of three established Shopify apps with a combined ARR of approximately $1.87M. The portfolio includes: Geo:Pro: Geolocation-based storefront personalization TrackiPal: PayPal tracking automation for Shopify merchants Easy Lockdown: Content and storefront access control Together, these are profitable, well-established products with engaged customer bases. They're not hypergrowth startups, but well-run businesses with clear opportunities to improve the product experience, strengthen operations and continue growing over time. As the portfolio has grown, it's reached the point where I need an experienced operator to lead the day-to-day, keep the business running smoothly and turn strategy into execution. The role is fully remote, async-friendly and suited to someone who enjoys ownership, autonomy and building well-run businesses. What you'd own Team coordination and delivery: Run the day-to-day by coordinating the developer and tester through the full delivery cycle - from spec → build → ship → measure - keeping everyone aligned across time zones and hiring additional contractors as needed. Roadmap and prioritization: We'll set the roadmap together. I'll be closely involved at first, and over time this becomes increasingly your call. Turn Amplitude data, review themes and support signals into a prioritized backlog in Linear, and write clear tickets for the developer. Metrics and experimentation: Own the analytics story. Understand what moved, what didn't and what to try next. Design experiments and report on impact. Quality and documentation: Continually raise the bar on user experience through better documentation, smoother onboarding, fewer rough edges. Platform stewardship: Stay ahead of Shopify API changes, manage App Store compliance reviews and lead our annual Built for Shopify review to retain BFS status. Support oversight and escalations: Our support agency handles tier-1 tickets. You're the escalation point for product and engineering issues and own the agency relationship, ensuring response times, ticket quality and the merchant experience meet the bar. Shopify App Store Paid Ads: Oversee existing paid advertising campaigns, working with our marketing contractor to ensure everything runs smoothly. We'll set the marketing budget together each quarter, and you'll manage it. Shopify App Store rankings: Monitor Shopify App Store rankings across the portfolio, identify opportunities to improve rankings and respond quickly when rankings decline. What you don't have to do Write code (there's a developer for that) Do QA (there's a tester for that) Handle routine support tickets (an agency handles that) Respond to reviews (a contractor handles that) Fundraise, hire executives, sit in stakeholder meetings or manage political overhead - none of that exists here Growth areas we've already identified Easy Lockdown: Shift to usage-based pricing Geo:Pro + Easy Lockdown: Onboarding and activation optimization Geo:Pro + Easy Lockdown: Feature gaps that address missing customer use cases All three apps: Lift review ratings to improve organic App Store rankings You're not walking into a blank page - there's already a clear direction, but plenty of room to test your own ideas. What you'll be walking into Small, remote team: You'll be coordinating a small team of contractors working across different time zones, so communication and keeping work moving are a big part of the role. Established products: The apps are profitable and well established, but some of the codebases are older and occasionally require pragmatic workarounds rather than perfect solutions. Data-driven decisions: Our analytics stack is solid (Amplitude, BigQuery, Shopify Partners) - SQL fluency, or comfort writing it with AI help, is required. How we'll work together Founder involvement: I've run these apps alongside another business and know them inside out. I'll stay focused on product direction, strategy, quarterly planning and major decisions while you run the day-to-day. Working rhythm: We'll meet weekly at first while we build context and alignment, then move to monthly strategy check-ins and quarterly planning sessions. Beyond that, you'll have the autonomy to run with it. Who you are Strong operator: You've successfully run product or delivery for a small SaaS team. Background isn't important - results are. Technically fluent: You can write clear product specs, understand trade-offs and weigh development estimates without needing to review code. Organized and proactive: You enjoy coordinating people, removing blockers and making sure nothing falls through the cracks. Data-driven: You use Amplitude, SQL and customer feedback to inform decisions. Self-directed: You're comfortable working asynchronously, managing your own priorities and taking ownership without constant direction. Bonus: Experience in the Shopify ecosystem, App Store Optimization (ASO), paid acquisition or SaaS growth. Where this could go This isn't a role with a fixed ceiling. As you build context, take on more responsibility and the portfolio grows, there's scope for the role to grow too. Exactly what that looks like will depend on the business and the impact you have, but the door is genuinely open. Assume you've had one week to get oriented - what would you focus on first, what would you want to understand, and how would you decide what to work on? Email your Loom to: apply@geoproapp.com I'll personally review every application. If your Loom is a strong fit, I'll invite you to a short introductory interview. If that goes well, we'll schedule a final, more in-depth interview before making an offer. To apply: https://weworkremotely.com/remote-jobs/geopro-labs-inc-head-of-operations-shopify-app-portfolio

record.evidence_text: Headquarters: Orlando, FL URL: https://profitablepaintercpa.com/careers Tax Preparer Join Our Team Are you an experienced tax preparer who enjoys solving problems, working with small business owners, and producing accurate, high-quality tax returns? Join Profitable Painter CPA PLLC, a fast-growing, tech-enabled, remote-first CPA firm that exclusively serves painting contractors across the U.S. and Canada. Our mission is simple: guide painting contractors to financial prosperity. We’re looking for a seasoned Tax Preparer who loves tax preparation, pays close attention to the details, embraces technology, and wants the stability of a year-round position with a collaborative CPA firm. You’ll work closely with our Tax Manager and tax reviewers to prepare individual and business tax returns, communicate with clients, resolve routine tax questions, and keep returns moving efficiently through our paperless tax workflow. What You’ll Do Prepare accurate and timely federal and state individual and business tax returns, including: Individual returns (Form 1040), including Schedules C, E, and D/Form 8949 Rental property and investment reporting Partnership returns (Form 1065) S Corporation returns (Form 1120S) C Corporation returns (Form 1120) Straightforward multi-state individual and business returns K-1 reporting from partnerships, S corporations, and trusts Common individual tax credits and deductions Basic Section 199A/QBI calculations Depreciation, Section 179, and bonus depreciation Basic Schedule M-1 and M-2 reconciliations Review your own work for completeness, accuracy, and internal consistency before submitting returns for reviewer sign-off. Identify potential issues involving shareholder or partner basis, multi-state taxation, or other areas requiring reviewer or Tax Manager involvement. Research routine tax questions independently using firm resources, recognize when an issue should be escalated, and collaborate with the reviewer or Tax Manager on more complex or unusual tax matters. Communicate directly with clients regarding tax questions, missing information, and outstanding documents. Document client communication and maintain accurate workflow status updates within TaxDome. Collaborate with tax reviewers and the Tax Manager to resolve questions and complete returns efficiently. Stay current on federal and state tax law changes and participate in regular tax department meetings and training. Look for opportunities to improve the efficiency and quality of our tax preparation process. Why You’ll Love Working Here Fully Remote: Work from anywhere in the world. Year-Round: This is not just a seasonal tax position. Join a growing firm with stable, ongoing work throughout the year. Modern Tech Stack: Work in a streamlined, paperless environment using Drake Tax, TaxDome, Juno, Verito, Slack, Notion, and other technology designed to make tax preparation more efficient. Collaborative Tax Team: Work closely with experienced reviewers and our Tax Manager rather than being left to figure everything out on your own. Professional Growth: Receive ongoing feedback, training, and opportunities to strengthen your technical tax knowledge. Core Values – A.C.E.: Accountability: Do what you say you’ll do. Collaboration: We win as a team. Excellence: Always push for better—for yourself and our clients. Mission-Driven: Help hardworking painting contractors thrive financially and build stronger businesses. Supportive Team: We’re organized, forward-thinking, technology-focused, and genuinely care about providing an exceptional experience for our clients and teammates. Compensation & Benefits Varying Compensation (depending on experience) Flat Rate per return equivalent to $12-25 USD per hour Health Reimbursement Arrangement (HRA) (U.S. Only) SIMPLE IRA retirement plan with employer matching (U.S. Only) Paid Time Off Paid Holidays Ongoing training and professional development Professional, collaborative remote work environment You’re a Great Fit If You Have: 2+ years of public accounting or tax preparation experience A CPA, EA, or equivalent tax preparation experience (preferred) Experience preparing both individual and business tax returns, including familiarity with Forms 1040, 1065, 1120S, and 1120 Strong working knowledge of federal and state taxation Excellent analytical and problem-solving skills Exceptional attention to detail and a commitment to producing accurate, high-quality work Strong organizational skills and the ability to manage multiple priorities and deadlines effectively Comfort learning and working with technology-based platforms and processes A professional, positive, and client-focused approach The ability to work independently while collaborating effectively with a fully remote team Fluency in written and spoken English, with strong professional communication skills The ability to work a consistent schedule aligned with Eastern, Central, or Pacific U.S. business hours The drive, reliability, and availability to consistently work 40–48 hours per week as business needs require A reliable high-speed internet connection and dedicated home workspace The ability to maintain strict confidentiality of client and firm information What Success Looks Like You consistently prepare accurate, complete, and high-quality tax returns while meeting production deadlines. You catch issues before returns reach the reviewer, incorporate feedback, and continue improving your technical skills over time. You communicate proactively with clients and teammates, keep your workflow current, and help returns move smoothly through the preparation and review process. Most importantly, you take pride in doing excellent work and contributing to a team that helps small business owners make smarter financial decisions. Ready to Join Our Tax Team? If you’re looking for a stable, fully remote tax career with a modern CPA firm that embraces technology, invests in its employees, and values quality over simply pushing returns out the door, we’d love to hear from you. Apply today and take the next step in your tax career with Profitable Painter CPA. Go to the link below and complete the application: https://profitablepaintercpa.com/careers To apply: https://weworkremotely.com/remote-jobs/profitable-painter-cpa-pllc-tax-preparer-us
